newsitem.title: USA: Cleveland's one-time "Boy Mayor" seeks House seat.
newsitem.headline: Cleveland's one-time "Boy Mayor" seeks House seat.

text.p: Dennis Kucinich, the controversial "boy mayor" who presided over Cleveland's financial default two decades ago, is in a tough race to regain for the Democrats a House seat they held for years.

Kucinich is up against second-term Republican Martin Hoke in a district that ranges from Cleveland's blue-collar west side to upscale suburbs. Both Kucinich's City Hall past and Hoke's support for House Speaker Newt Gingrich have been issues in the race, though by no means the only ones.

Kucinich, now 50, was elected mayor in 1977 at age 31. A few confrontational months later Cleveland became the first major U.S. city since the Great Depression to default when it could not pay about $15 million in bank loans initiated by a previous mayor.
Kucinich was drummed out of office at the end of his two-year term. He returned to public life in the 1980s as a city councilman and is now a state legislator.

Kucinich told Reuters recently that local banks, mad at his dogged refusal to sell Cleveland's municipal light system to an investor-owned electric company, refused to extend credit and forced the infamous default. The banks shared directors and interests with the utility firm, he said.

Kucinich, whose campaign slogan is "Light Up Congress with Kucinich," said: "History has proven me right. The municipal power system survived and has expanded ... and held down electric rates and saved jobs."
Hoke, a lawyer and businessman, ousted 16-year veteran Democrat Mary Rose Oakar in 1992 after she was caught up in the House Bank scandal.
Hoke was re-elected in 1994 when Republicans gained control of the House and Senate despite an on-camera gaffe in which he commented about a woman television producer's breasts. He later apologised.
Whether Republicans maintain their 235-198 House majority will depend on whether they win close races like this one.

Kucinich could be helped by President Clinton's strength in Ohio. A poll conducted for Reuters by John Zogby Group International and released Wednesday showed Clinton with more than an 11-point lead over Bob Dole in the key state.

In addition, a University of Cincinnati poll out Wednesday said there has been a shift in recent days that favours Democratic House candidaes in Ohio generally, though swing voters still favour Republican congressional candidates.
Hoke, 44, says most of Kucinich's campaign is financed by "Washington special interests," which a spokesman said meant national labour unions. Hoke also defended his voting record.
"The question isn't whether I voted with Gingrich or voted against Gingrich," he said. "The real question is did I vote with the district I represent."

In a recent debate Hoke said Kucinich was trying to scare senior citizens with "vile demagoguery" about Republican efforts to slow Medicare growth, then warned that Kucinich has said he wants to raise Social Security taxes.
"I haven't," Kucinich retorted, calling Hoke a millionaire who will endanger Medicare, Social Security and pension funds.

On another evening the two dueled at campaign events in the same condominium complex where Hoke lives, a suburban high-rise in a neighbourhood called the Gold Coast on the Lake Erie shore. Kucinich lives in Cleveland.
Hoke moved easily among a friendly crowd of about 70, sipping Diet Coke from crystal at a "meet your neighbour" gathering at a supporter's elegant 15th-floor condominium.
Kucinich was downstairs in the party room, meeting 50 or so people sitting on folding chairs.

Hoke event host William Flynn said, "I'm not a party voter. I support Mr. Hoke because I like his platform and I like what he stands for. I am somewhat disdainful of his opponent because I remember Mr. Kucinich as mayor of Cleveland and remember all the problems of the city then."
In those days, some called Kucinich an urban populist. Others called him confrontational and unwilling to compromise.
Now, he told those in the party room, he seeks to avoid "polarized thinking" and to "approach, in a more holistic fashion, politics which seek unity."
